# Compress Video

- Route: `/tools/compress-video`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `video`
- Slug: `compress-video`

## Summary

Shrink MP4, WebM, MOV, MKV, and AVI files for the web, email, social, and cloud uploads. (Video tools)

## Details

A video file is large because of its bitrate: how many bits the encoder spent per second of footage. Phones and screen recorders spend generously, which is why a short 1080p clip can run to tens or hundreds of megabytes. This page opens a three-control compressor instead of the full converter: a compression level, an output container, and an optional resolution and codec. On our server the job is one FFmpeg command that re-encodes the picture at a constant-quality setting (CRF) chosen by the level, re-encodes the audio to AAC or Opus, and writes the result with the index at the front of the file so it starts playing before it has fully downloaded.
### What it does
- Re-encodes the video at a fixed quality level rather than a fixed bitrate: Smallest file is CRF 31, Balanced is CRF 26 and High quality is CRF 22.
- Outputs MP4 (H.264 by default, or H.265/HEVC when you pick it) or WebM (VP9 with Opus audio).
- Optionally scales the picture down to 1080p, 720p or 480p in the same pass while keeping the aspect ratio.
- Optionally drops the audio track entirely for the smallest possible file.
- Accepts MP4, MOV, M4V, WebM, MKV, AVI, FLV, WMV, MPEG and MPG uploads; the full converter page handles ProRes and other editing formats.
### How to use it
1. Upload the video: The browser puts the file straight into our storage bucket, then asks the API to start the job.
2. Choose a level: Balanced is preselected. Smallest file trades visible detail for size; High quality keeps more of it.
3. Optionally change format, resolution or codec: MP4 with H.264 plays everywhere; H.265 and WebM are smaller on devices that decode them.
4. FFmpeg re-encodes: libx264, libx265 or libvpx-vp9 with the CRF for your level, plus AAC or Opus audio and faststart for MP4.
5. Download the smaller file: The result stays in the job folder until its retention window ends.
### Technical details
- The exact command for MP4 is ffmpeg -i input [-vf scale=-1:H] -c:v libx264 -crf N -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart -c:a aac output.mp4, where N is 31, 26 or 22 for the three levels (buildVideoCodecArgs and videoCRF in converter.go). No encoder speed preset is passed, so libx264 runs at its default, medium.
- Picking H.265 swaps the encoder for libx265 and adds -tag:v hvc1, the tag QuickTime and Safari need to recognise HEVC inside MP4. Older Android phones, smart TVs and many web players cannot decode H.265 at all.
- WebM output runs libvpx-vp9 with -b:v 0 -crf N and Opus audio; if the server FFmpeg build lacked VP9 or Opus it would fall back to VP8 and Vorbis. The same N is passed, but VP9 reads CRF on a 0 to 63 scale, so 26 is a relatively high quality setting there.
- A resolution choice becomes scale=-1:1080, scale=-1:720 or scale=-1:480: height fixed, width computed from the source aspect ratio. The height is applied as given, so picking 1080p for a 720p source upscales it and makes the file larger, not smaller; pick a height at or below the source.
- Remove the audio track adds -an. Otherwise the audio is re-encoded by the FFmpeg native AAC encoder at its default bitrate (no -b:a is passed; for stereo that is typically about 128 kbps), which is a small fraction of the file at any level.
- Compression is CRF-driven, so the output size follows the content: static slides compress far harder than confetti or water. The server validates CRF to 0 to 51 and the compression level to one of the three names before any encoding starts.
- The upload is also queued for the automated content analysis that every standard conversion receives: frames are sampled and described by a local vision model, and audio is transcribed on our own hardware. The analysis result is stored with the job, not shared.
### When not to use it
Do not compress a file you still intend to edit or colour grade; every re-encode loses detail, and an editor wants the original or a ProRes intermediate from the full converter instead. Do not use it to make a clip play on a particular device if the problem is the container rather than the size; the video converter changes formats without lowering quality. If your only goal is to cut a section out, the trimmer copies the streams without re-encoding and is both faster and lossless. And if the file is large because it is long, compression helps less than you hope; a 20 minute recording at CRF 26 is still a 20 minute recording.
### Use cases
- Email and chat: Get a 1 minute phone recording under a 25 MB or 100 MB limit without a separate sharing link.
- Website hero and background loops: Encode a WebM or H.264 MP4 that a page can autoplay without a long buffer.
- Course and meeting recordings: Shrink screen recordings whose static slides compress extremely well at any CRF.
- Archive copies: Keep a 720p Balanced copy of long originals and move the master to cold storage.
### FAQ
Q: Will compressing make my video look worse?
A: Some detail is always lost in a re-encode. At High quality (CRF 22) and Balanced (CRF 26) the loss is mostly in fine grain and noise that most viewers do not notice; at Smallest file (CRF 31) you can see softening on detailed footage. Keeping the resolution avoids the blurring that downscaling adds.
Q: Should I pick H.264, H.265 or WebM?
A: H.264 MP4 plays on everything, including old TVs and corporate laptops. H.265 gives a smaller file at the same CRF but needs a device that decodes HEVC; we tag it hvc1 so Apple players accept it. WebM (VP9 and Opus) is the choice for web pages where you control the player.
Q: How much smaller will the file be?
A: It depends on the source bitrate and the content. A phone clip at 12 Mbps has a lot of headroom and shrinks dramatically at CRF 26; a file that was already encoded at a modest bitrate shrinks little, because CRF spends what the picture needs. Dropping to 720p and removing audio always help.
Q: Does the compressor add a watermark or change the frame rate?
A: No. The frame rate, duration and aspect ratio are preserved, and nothing is drawn on the picture. Only the codec, the CRF, the optional height and the optional audio removal change.
Q: Is compressing a video free, and what are the limits?
A: Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. A compression that fails is refunded. The current numbers are on the pricing page.
Q: Why is the output not smaller than the original?
A: The source was probably already compressed efficiently, or it is at a low bitrate for its resolution. CRF cannot go below what the picture requires without a lower level. Try Smallest file, or drop the resolution, or switch to H.265.
Q: Can I compress a video with no audio or keep the original audio untouched?
A: A silent source stays silent. Audio in a kept track is always re-encoded to AAC (MP4) or Opus (WebM) by this page; the full video converter is where you set an explicit audio bitrate.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Send visitors here when a video file is too big and they want it smaller for email, the web, social or cloud uploads: "shrink this video", "my phone clip is too large", "make an MP4 smaller". It re-encodes MP4, WebM, MOV, MKV or AVI at a chosen quality level and can scale down to 1080p, 720p or 480p.
When to send them elsewhere: If only the format is the problem, use Video Converter (video-converter); to cut a section out, Video Trimmer (video-trimmer) is faster and lossless. For adaptive streaming packages, use Transcode Video to HLS (transcode-to-hls) or Transcode Video to DASH (transcode-to-dash).
Related tools: video-trimmer (cut length instead of re-encoding); video-converter (change container or codec without targeting size); resize-video (change the picture dimensions); transcode-to-hls (build a streaming ladder instead of one file)
